newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli capital movements fell 44 percent in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Israeli capital movements fell 44 percent in 1996.

text.p: Capital movements into and out of Israel fell 44 percent to $4.36 billion last year from $7.89 billion in 1995, as capital imports by the Israeli private sector slowed, the Bank of Israel said on Tuesday.
It said net capital imports by foreigners rose 18 percent to $2.60 billion last year, while net capital imports by Israelis fell to $1.77 billion from $5.69 billion.

"These changes ... reflect an increase in the weighting of those capital imports unaffected by short-term interest rates differentials between the shekel and foreign currencies from 38 percent of the total in 1995 to 51 percent in 1996," the central bank said.
It attributed the decline in rate-sensitive capital inflows to increased expectations of devaluation in the Israeli currency during most of last year.

The central bank said devaluation expectations had fallen this year, spurring renewed capital imports in the form of private sector foreign currency loans. It estimated these reached $1.5 billion this year.
"As a result the Bank of Israel has been forced to purchase foreign currency to defend the lower end of the currency trading band," the central bank said.
The report comes as the Bank of Israel faces sharp criticism for encouraging capital inflows through its restrictive monetary policy and high interest rates.
Treasury officials and others have said capital inflows have not allowed the Israeli currency to depreciate in line with inflation, hurting the country's export competitiveness.

The Bank of Israel said the sharp rise in capital imports by foreigners was due to the big increase in Israeli public offerings overseas. Foreigners invested $761 million in Israeli overseas offerings last year, up from $326 million in 1995.
Foreign direct investment, by contrast, rose slightly to $1.25 billion from $1.22 billion in 1995.
